pedagogy.summary:
- **Age:** 11–12 years

- **Topic:** Speed & Distance-Time Graphs

- **Standards — UK (DfE National Curriculum, KS3 Physics — Motion):** Speed and the quantitative relationship between average speed, distance and time (speed = distance ÷ time); the representation of a journey on a distance–time graph and the gradient of a straight segment as speed.

- **Standards — US (NGSS MS SEP — Using Mathematics and Computational Thinking):** Use mathematical representations to describe and predict an object's motion (speed as distance ÷ time); supports MS-PS2 Motion and Stability and CCSS-Math 6.RP/7.RP ratios and proportional relationships.

- **Operational details:** This topic is the quantitative heart of motion: calculating average speed with speed = distance ÷ time, attaching correct units (m/s, km/h), and tying that number to the gradient of a distance-time graph. The most effective sequencing, per Oak National Academy, builds from distance = speed × time FIRST ('metres per second means metres travelled each second'), because the multiplicative form is more intuitive than the division form. The deeper goal is proportional reasoning — understanding speed as the rate that links distance and time — so representations that expose the proportional structure (double number lines, ratio tables) are preferred over rote use of the 'formula triangle', which research shows can block more productive reasoning. Average speed must be taught as TOTAL distance ÷ TOTAL time (including any stationary periods), not the mean of the separate speeds.

- **Checkpoint:** Tier B (transitional/early-formal). Calculating average speed rests on emerging proportional reasoning: pupils build from distance = speed × time, attach units (m/s), and connect the value to a graph's gradient. The key threshold at 11–12 is defining average speed as TOTAL distance ÷ TOTAL time — including stationary periods — rather than averaging the separate speeds, and reasoning proportionally (double number lines, ratio tables) instead of leaning on the formula triangle as a substitute for understanding.
bestPractices: Teach distance = speed × time before speed = distance ÷ time; anchor on 'm/s = the number of metres travelled each second' (Oak National Academy).

Use double number lines and ratio tables (NCETM) to make the proportional relationship visible — e.g. scaling distance and time together to predict how far in a new time — rather than relying solely on the formula triangle, which can short-circuit reasoning.
Define average speed explicitly as total distance ÷ total time, including stopped periods; give journeys with stops so the 'mean of the speeds' error is confronted.
Connect the calculation to the graph: average speed of a straight segment IS its gradient; have pupils compute it both ways and reconcile.
Use precise language — qualify 'constant'/'steady' with a value ('a constant speed of 4 m/s') and always state units; keep distance distinct from displacement.
Use predict-then-calculate tasks (estimate the speed, then compute) and real contexts (cyclists, cars) to keep the abstraction grounded.
keyRepresentations: Double number line linking distance and time (NCETM) — the central proportional model
Ratio table for distance:time, scaled by a functional multiplier
Distance-time graph with gradient = average speed
The speed-distance-time 'formula triangle' (a memory aid, used with caution, not as a substitute for reasoning)
Unit unpacking: m/s as 'metres each second', km/h, mph
commonMisconceptions: Calculating average speed as the mean of the individual speeds rather than total distance ÷ total time (Third Space Learning).
Forgetting to include stationary periods in the total time when finding average speed.
Reading a value off the vertical axis and calling it the speed instead of finding the gradient.
Treating the formula triangle as the whole concept — procedural recall that blocks proportional reasoning (Susac et al., Phys. Rev. PER).
Language slips: 'constant speed' read as 'always moving', 'steady speed' as 'not too fast'; conflating distance with displacement (Oak National Academy).

learn.summary: For ages 11–12, teach average speed as a proportional rate linking distance and time, built up from distance = speed × time ('m/s means metres travelled each second') before introducing speed = distance ÷ time. The central threshold is that average speed = TOTAL distance ÷ TOTAL time, including any stationary periods — not the mean of the separate speeds (the mean is only correct when equal time is spent at each speed). Use double number lines and ratio tables to expose the proportional structure and support prediction, connect the calculation to the gradient of a distance-time graph (a single leg's speed is its segment gradient; the whole-journey average is the start-to-end chord gradient), and confront the 'mean of the speeds' and 'ignore the stop' errors directly. A journey-building activity with live, synchronised feedback is the richest approach; a quiz consolidates the procedure; a worked-example reference card scaffolds a single case.

activities.title: Build a journey and watch the average speed update
feedback: If a learner expects the average of 8 m/s and 4 m/s to be 6 m/s (which is correct here only because the two legs last equal times), show that after inserting a 20-second stop the average-speed readout drops below 6, because the stopped seconds are added to the total time while the distance does not grow.
When prediction and calculation disagree, point back to the running denominator: 'the cart is sitting still, but the total time keeps climbing — what does that do to distance ÷ time?'

If the learner reads a speed off the vertical axis, redirect them to compute the gradient (distance change ÷ time change) of a straight segment to get that leg's speed; for the whole-journey average, compare with the gradient of the line joining the start and end points rather than a single leg's gradient.
Reinforce correct units: the readout is in metres per second because you divided metres by seconds.
activities.rationale: Live, synchronised feedback (an animating cart, a drawing distance-time graph, and a running total-distance-over-total-time calculator) is intended to let learners feel speed as a trade-off between distance and time and work out the 'include the stops' rule rather than memorise it. The double number line keeps the proportional structure visible and supports prediction, which cited research associates with deeper understanding than formula-triangle recall. The animation, graph, double-number-line widget and challenge mode are suggested ways to make the mechanism concrete, not mandatory features; their effectiveness is untested here.
sourceClaims: Pupils find speed easier built from distance = speed × time first; 'm/s is the number of metres travelled each second'; 'constant'/'steady' speed language must be qualified with a value.
Double number lines and ratio tables make the proportional structure of compound measures (speed) visible and support prediction; a functional multiplier shows deep understanding.

Reliance on formulas can block more productive reasoning strategies; slope-height and iconic confusions are common; average speed is often mis-computed as the mean of speeds or by ignoring stationary periods.
learnerActions: Assemble a trip from segments, choosing a speed for each leg; for the core demonstration use two legs of EQUAL DURATION (e.g. a leg at 8 m/s then an equal-time leg at 4 m/s), and insert optional STOP blocks of a chosen duration.
Before inserting a 20-second stop between the two equal-duration legs, predict the average speed over the whole trip and write down your reasoning.
Insert the stop and observe how the average-speed readout changes; note whether it rose, fell, or stayed the same, and explain why.
Use a double-number-line widget beside the journey to predict: 'keeping this leg's speed, how far would you travel in 10 seconds?' by scaling distance and time together.
Attempt a challenge: adjust the journey to hit a target average speed when one stop is forced into the trip.

State the speed of a single leg with its units and check it against the gradient of that leg's straight segment on the distance-time graph; then note that the whole-journey average speed matches the gradient of the straight line joining the journey's start and end points (the chord), not any single intermediate segment.
activities.intendedInsight: Average speed = total distance ÷ total time, and stopped seconds still count in the denominator. With two equal-time legs the mean of the two speeds (here 6 m/s) is genuinely correct; but inserting a stop adds time without adding distance, so the average drops below it — showing that total time, including stops, is what matters. Speed is a proportional rate you can scale to predict new distances and times.

activities.title: Consolidate the calculation and graph reading
feedback: For the multi-leg item, confirm that the 'mean of the speeds' option is a distractor and reinforce total distance ÷ total time.
If a learner picks a steeper-looking segment that is actually less steep, prompt them to read off the actual distance and time changes rather than judging by eye.
Flag any answer where metres and seconds are mismatched with the stated unit.
activities.rationale: A checking activity makes the procedure crisply assessable across step types and is well suited as a follow-up that consolidates the calculation. Note that it mainly drills the procedure; it does less to build the proportional intuition than the journey-building activity, so use it after that work rather than instead of it.
sourceClaims: Reliance on formulas can block more productive reasoning strategies; slope-height and iconic confusions are common; average speed is often mis-computed as the mean of speeds or by ignoring stationary periods.
learnerActions: Fill in the missing quantity for distance = speed × time and for speed = distance ÷ time rearrangements, attaching correct units each time.
Read the speed of a straight distance-time graph segment by computing its gradient (distance change ÷ time change).
For a multi-leg journey that includes a stop, choose the correct average speed from options that include the 'mean of the speeds' answer, and justify the choice.
Order several graph sections from slowest to fastest by comparing their gradients.
activities.intendedInsight: The speed = distance ÷ time procedure can be applied reliably with correct units, average speed over a whole journey is not the mean of the leg speeds, and the gradient of a straight distance-time segment gives that leg's speed.

activities.title: Walk through a worked example as a reference card
feedback: If the learner forgets units, the card re-shows that dividing metres by seconds gives m/s.
If they divide in the wrong order, the card re-shows distance on top and time underneath.
activities.rationale: A step-revealing reference card scaffolds one worked case and reinforces units. It is a recap aid: because the quantities are fixed it cannot let the learner vary distance and time and feel the rate, so it under-serves the proportional core and should supplement, not replace, the hands-on journey work.
sourceClaims: Pupils find speed easier built from distance = speed × time first; 'm/s is the number of metres travelled each second'; 'constant'/'steady' speed language must be qualified with a value.
learnerActions: Step through one worked journey: reveal the total distance, reveal the total time, then reveal the division and the resulting speed with its units.
Note the unit reminder at each step (metres ÷ seconds = metres per second).
Use the card as a recap aid when stuck on a later calculation.
activities.intendedInsight: A single average-speed calculation follows a fixed, checkable sequence: identify total distance, identify total time, divide, and attach units.

activities.title: Measure and reconcile average speed in a real run
feedback: If learners predict the midpoint of the two speeds, highlight that the slow leg takes more seconds, so it carries more weight in the total time.
Connect the measured result back to the rule: total distance ÷ total time, with both legs' actual measured times summed.
activities.rationale: A predict-then-measure task in a real context grounds the abstraction and directly confronts the 'mean of the speeds' error using the learner's own measured times. It targets the same key misconception as the journey-builder through physical investigation. Because the legs are equal in distance (not time), the midpoint over-estimates the true average — a useful contrast with the equal-time case.
sourceClaims: Reliance on formulas can block more productive reasoning strategies; slope-height and iconic confusions are common; average speed is often mis-computed as the mean of speeds or by ignoring stationary periods.
learnerActions: Mark two equal 10 m stretches. Have one person jog the first and walk the second while others time each leg.
Before calculating, predict the average speed over the whole 20 m and say WHY.
Calculate average speed from the measured times as total distance ÷ total time, and compare it with your prediction.

Work out each leg's speed from its measured time (10 m ÷ that leg's time), find the midpoint of those two speeds, and discuss why the whole-run average (20 m ÷ total time) is lower than that midpoint whenever the jogging leg was faster than the walking leg.
activities.intendedInsight: Over two equal-distance legs, more time is spent on the slower (walking) leg, so the true average speed is pulled below the simple midpoint of the two speeds — the average is weighted by time spent, not by distance.

constraints: Teach distance = speed × time before speed = distance ÷ time, anchored on 'm/s = metres travelled each second'.
Define average speed explicitly as total distance ÷ total time, including stopped periods; always give at least one journey with a stop so the 'mean of the speeds' error is confronted.

The mean of the two leg speeds equals the true average when equal time is spent at each speed; for equal-distance legs at different speeds the true (time-weighted) average is lower than the mean. State the leg configuration whenever a specific average value is claimed.

Connect calculation to graphs precisely: a single leg's speed equals the gradient of its straight segment, while the whole-journey average speed equals the gradient of the straight line joining the journey's start and end points — not any single intermediate segment.
Use double number lines and ratio tables to make the proportional relationship visible; treat the formula triangle only as a cautious memory aid, never as a substitute for proportional reasoning.
Use precise language: qualify 'constant'/'steady' speed with a value (e.g. 'a constant speed of 4 m/s'), always state units, and keep distance distinct from displacement.

The step-revealing reference card and the quiz are scaffolds/consolidation: they drill or display a fixed procedure and do not let learners vary quantities to feel the rate, so they should supplement, not replace, hands-on proportional work.

Suggested interactive features (animating cart, live-drawing graph, running denominator readout, double-number-line widget, draggable segments, challenge mode) are illustrative ways to make the mechanism concrete, not required components, and their efficacy is untested.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.

Source-field arithmetic check: the diagnostic answer of ~2.86 m/s is correct for two EQUAL-DISTANCE 100 m legs at 5 m/s and 2 m/s (times 20 s and 50 s; 200 m ÷ 70 s ≈ 2.857 m/s). However, the assessment's poeTask describes two 10 m stretches (20 m total) while the correctAnswer narrative uses 100 m legs (200 m total). The numeric method is sound, but the distances are inconsistent between fields — resolve the scenario distances before using with learners. The measure-and-reconcile activity uses the 10 m/20 m poeTask framing and leaves exact numbers to be computed from measured times.

Coherence fix applied to activity 1: the '8 and 4 m/s average 6, then drops after a stop' demonstration is only valid for equal-time legs, so the activity specifies equal-duration legs; otherwise the pre-stop average is already below 6 and the narrative would be inconsistent.

Gradient fix applied to activity 1: an earlier draft told learners to check the whole-journey average speed against 'the matching straight segment'. Because a single segment's gradient is only that leg's speed, the actions and feedback now distinguish a single leg (segment gradient) from the whole-journey average (start-to-end chord gradient).
The car example (60 km, stop for 1 hour, 60 km in 1 hour) gives 120 km ÷ 3 h = 40 km/h; verify this is presented consistently if used.

Several sources are marked unverified in the original row (NCETM representations; Susac et al./Third Space Learning); confidence was legacy-'high' but is not independently re-established here. The claim that formula-triangle reliance 'blocks' reasoning reflects cited research tendencies, not a universal law; present it as a caution.

The original ruled out 3D and conversation formats as adding nothing / not advancing the content; these are treated as scope-limited notes (those media do not themselves illuminate the numeric/proportional structure or require an in-role dimension) rather than universal claims, and were not carried as learner-facing restrictions.

assess.poeTask: Mark two equal 10 m stretches. Have a student jog the first and walk the second while others time each leg. Ask the class to predict the average speed over the whole 20 m, and WHY, before calculating from the measured times. Predicting the midpoint of the two speeds is the diagnostic tell; the measured total-distance-over-total-time result coming out lower (more time spent walking) is the payoff.
probeDeeper: If the runner had spent EQUAL TIME (not equal distance) at 5 and 2 m/s, would 3.5 be right then? Why?
A car drives 60 km in 1 hour, stops for 1 hour, then drives 60 km in another hour. What's its average speed over the whole trip?
Which section of a distance-time graph shows the fastest speed, and how do you get a number from it?
What units should your average speed be in, and how do you know?
assess.correctAnswer: No, 3.5 m/s is wrong. Average speed = TOTAL distance ÷ TOTAL time, not the mean of the two speeds. The first 100 m takes 100/5 = 20 s; the second takes 100/2 = 50 s. Total 200 m in 70 s gives an average of about 2.86 m/s. It's below 3.5 because the runner spends MORE time going slowly.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'Average speed is just the mean of the speeds — halfway between them.'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Define average speed = total distance ÷ total time; compute the two times to show the result is weighted by time spent, not distance.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Gives (5+2)/2 = 3.5 with no reference to the times.

errorPatterns.pattern: 'When there's a stop, only count the time spent moving.'
errorPatterns.nextMove: Total time includes stops; a stop lowers the average speed over the whole trip.
errorPatterns.revealedBy: For a journey with a stop, divides distance by the moving-time only.

errorPatterns.nextMove: Build speed = distance ÷ time from a double number line / ratio table rather than a magic triangle; check units (m/s = metres per second).
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Multiplies instead of dividing, or mis-rearranges the formula triangle.

responseLevels.gap: Averages the two speeds (3.5), or divides distance by moving-time only; may multiply distance by time.
responseLevels.full: Computes average speed as total distance ÷ total time (including stopped time), explains why time spent at each speed weights the result (so the answer is below the midpoint), and reads/represents it on a distance-time graph, with correct units.
responseLevels.partial: Knows speed = distance ÷ time and can find a single-section speed, but for a two-part journey still averages the speeds or forgets to use TOTAL time — applies the formula per section without combining correctly.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: A runner covers the first 100 m at 5 m/s, then walks the next 100 m at 2 m/s. A friend says 'the average speed is 3.5 m/s — halfway between 5 and 2'. Is that right? What is the average speed, and how should you work it out?
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: The signature error is averaging the two speeds (mean of 5 and 2). A student who understands says average speed = total distance ÷ total time, gets about 2.86, and explains that more time is spent at the slower speed so the average is pulled down. A student with the misconception gives 3.5 and can't say why the time spent at each speed matters. Tier 2 (how you work it out) is decisive.
